TOPICS.title: Absorbance and Concentration
TOPICS.overview: Absorbance measures attenuation on a logarithmic scale. In the linear Beer–Lambert range it is proportional to concentration and path length. This lesson keeps fractions, percentages and physical units distinct so that the algebra matches the measurement.

DERIVATIONS.not_applicable: This introductory topic uses an explicit definition and a worked check; no additional derivation or quantitative figure is required.

DEFS.text: Negative base-ten logarithm of fractional transmittance.

POINTS.text: Use the fractional transmittance in the logarithm. The illustrative coefficient is not a universal value for copper(II).

WHY.q: Why must fractional transmittance be used in the logarithm?
WHY.a: The definition uses I divided by I0. A percentage is one hundred times that ratio and would shift the logarithm by two.

FORMULAS.title: Beer–Lambert relation
FORMULAS.gives: Absorbance of a dilute absorbing species, such as illustrative $\ce{Cu^2+}$ in solution.
FORMULAS.when: Monochromatic measurement in the linear range with a suitable blank and consistent units.

SYMBOLS.name: Optical path length

SYMBOLS.name: Concentration
SYMBOLS.meaning: Amount of absorbing species per unit solution volume.

SYMBOLS.name: Fractional transmittance
SYMBOLS.meaning: Ratio $I/I_0$; use the fraction, not its percentage.

SYMBOLS.name: Transmitted and incident intensities
SYMBOLS.meaning: Both intensities use the same wavelength, geometry and units; their ratio is dimensionless.
